summary: Extends POP3 to support unencoded international characters in user names, passwords, addresses, message headers, and protocol error text. It is an Experimental protocol and was replaced by RFC 6856.

eli5.summary: Older email systems struggled with letters outside the basic English alphabet. This extension lets the mailbox protocol use names and messages in many languages directly. It was replaced by RFC 6856.

subtitle: Bringing international characters to the email retrieval protocol.

tldr.problem: POP3, the standard protocol for retrieving email from servers, only supports ASCII characters in user names, passwords, and message text. People in other parts of the world need to send and receive mail with their own alphabets.
tldr.mechanism: This specification adds two capabilities: a LANG command for servers to send error messages in the user's preferred language, and a UTF8 command that puts the session in UTF-8 mode, allowing international characters in headers and optional support for international user names and passwords.
tldr.outcome: Mail servers can now work with international characters natively, letting users read messages with their own writing systems. It was replaced by RFC 6856, which improved the approach.

today: RFC 6856 obsoleted this specification, providing an improved approach to UTF-8 in POP3. This RFC is Experimental and no longer recommended for new deployment.

sections.title: Introduction and the UTF-8 Email Challenge
sections.content:
POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) is the standard way client programs fetch email from mail servers. But it was designed in the 1980s when the Internet spoke only ASCII—the 127 basic English characters. People in Japan, Russia, China, India and everywhere else who write in their own alphabets had a problem: the protocol rejected their mail.

This specification extends POP3 to handle UTF-8, a way of encoding all the world's written languages as bytes. The changes are backward compatible: old clients still work, and new clients can opt in to UTF-8 by sending a command.

The specification is part of the broader Email Address Internationalization (EAI) work that extends email systems end-to-end. It defines two new capabilities: one for language negotiation and one for UTF-8 mode.
sections.eli5: Email used to only speak English. This adds the ability to use any alphabet. Old programs still work fine, and new ones can ask the server to switch to international mode.

sections.title: UTF-8 and the Internationalization Mechanism
sections.content:
UTF-8 is a way to encode any of the 100,000+ characters in Unicode (which includes every modern writing system) as a sequence of bytes. ASCII letters are still one byte, but accented letters, non-Latin alphabets, and other symbols take more.

POP3 extensions are negotiated using capabilities. When a client connects, the server sends a list of optional features it supports. The client can then request the ones it needs. This specification adds two new capabilities that allow clients to enable UTF-8 and choose a language for human-readable messages.

The downgrade problem is also important: when a message containing UTF-8 reaches an old mail server that does not support it, the message must be converted to ASCII using encoded-word syntax (as defined in RFC 2047). Clients reading downgraded messages need strategies to show the original text when possible.
sections.eli5: UTF-8 is a code that lets computers write any alphabet. POP3 lets clients ask servers which special features they support. The server can say it handles UTF-8 and many languages.

sections.title: Language Negotiation with the LANG Command
sections.content:
The LANG command allows clients to ask the server to use a specific language for human-readable text in responses. For example, a client from Spain might ask for Spanish error messages.

Servers that support LANG must advertise it as a capability. If a client sends LANG es, the server looks for a Spanish language tag in its supported list. If found, the server replies with +OK es followed by a message in Spanish. The message is sent in UTF-8.

A client can send LANG with no argument to request a list of all supported languages. The server returns each language tag (like en, de, ja) followed optionally by a description in that language itself. The default language is always i-default, used if the client does not send a LANG command or requests an unsupported language.
sections.eli5: The LANG command is like telling the mailbox: please speak to me in Portuguese. The server sends back a list of languages it knows, and switches to whichever you pick.

sections.title: UTF-8 Mode and Message Content
sections.content:
The UTF8 command has no arguments; sending it simply switches the session to UTF-8 mode. In UTF-8 mode, messages in a native UTF-8 mailstore are sent to the client as-is, with UTF-8 characters visible in headers and body. Outside UTF-8 mode, UTF-8 messages must be downconverted to 7-bit format to comply with traditional POP3 and SMTP rules.

The UTF8 capability response may include a USER argument. If present, this signals that the server accepts UTF-8 in the USER and PASS commands (usernames and passwords). When UTF-8 is used in authentication, the server applies SASLprep, a string-processing rule that normalizes and validates Unicode text. This is important to prevent spoofing and security problems.

The specification notes that even in UTF-8 mode, MIME binary encoding is still not permitted in POP3. Messages must be 7-bit or 8-bit. The list of messages and their sizes reported by the LIST command should match the bytes actually sent by RETR, though the specification acknowledges that servers sometimes report estimates when messages are downconverted.
sections.eli5: UTF8 is a simple command that tells the mailbox: send me messages as-is with all their international characters. If the server knows it, it can also accept your name and password in your own alphabet.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Concerns
sections.content:
Using UTF-8 in authentication (user names and passwords) introduces complexity. The server must correctly apply SASLprep to prevent invalid or dangerous characters from being accepted. Both servers and clients that support APOP (a related authentication method) must apply SASLprep to usernames and passwords used in digest calculations.

The LANG * command is a potential privacy leak: an attacker can send it and observe whether the server switches to a preferred language, which might reveal the user's location or preferences. Servers must have configuration options to prevent this.

Another subtle risk is incorrect reporting of message sizes after downconversion. If a client allocates a buffer based on the reported size and the actual message is larger, the client could crash or behave unpredictably. Servers are advised to report accurate sizes, or to err on the side of reporting larger sizes.

Finally, carefully implementing UTF-8 and SASLprep support in authentication code requires care to avoid introducing new parsing vulnerabilities or buffer overflows.
sections.eli5: Using foreign alphabets in passwords is tricky and risky. Servers must be careful not to leak which language a user prefers, and must not trick clients by reporting wrong message sizes.
